title: MLPC 03 - Density Estimation
subject: Machine Learning and Pattern Classification
description: Covers likelihood and maximum-likelihood estimation, Gaussian and Naive Bayes classifiers, nearest-neighbour and kernel density estimation, k-NN classification, scaling, and dimensionality. All questions are single-choice and modeled after the conceptual style of the MLPC Retry 2024S exam. Source: 03_Density_Estimation.pdf.

questions.question: What is the defining assumption of parametric density estimation?

options.text: The distribution belongs to a chosen family described by finitely many parameters
Every training point defines a separate class
The density must be estimated only at test points
No assumption about distribution shape is permitted

questions.explanation: Parametric estimation selects a distribution family and learns its unknown parameters.

questions.question: How does non-parametric density estimation differ from parametric estimation?

options.text: It fixes a Gaussian shape for every class
It estimates density locally without committing to one fixed global family
It requires no training examples
It can only be used with discrete features

questions.explanation: Non-parametric methods use the observed sample directly to estimate local density.

questions.question: For i.i.d. observations \(\mathcal{D}=\{\mathbf{x}_1,\ldots,\mathbf{x}_n\}\), the likelihood \(L(\theta:\mathcal{D})\) is:

options.text: The sum of the parameters
\(\prod_i p(\mathbf{x}_i\mid\theta)\)
A posterior distribution over classes
The probability \(P(\theta\mid\mathcal{D})\)

questions.explanation: Independence allows the joint probability or density of the sample to factor into a product.

questions.question: Why is log-likelihood commonly optimized instead of likelihood?

options.text: It changes the maximizing parameter
It turns products into sums and improves numerical stability
It makes negative densities valid
It normalizes the parameter distribution

questions.explanation: The logarithm is monotonic, preserves the argmax, and avoids tiny products.

questions.question: Which statement correctly distinguishes \(p(\mathbf{x}\mid\theta)\) from \(L(\theta:\mathcal{D})\)?

options.text: Both are necessarily normalized densities over \(\theta\)
\(p(\mathbf{x}\mid\theta)\) varies with \(\mathbf{x}\), while likelihood varies with \(\theta\) after \(\mathcal{D}\) is fixed
Likelihood is a class label
\(p(\mathbf{x}\mid\theta)\) can only be discrete

questions.explanation: The same model expression is viewed as a function of observations for a density and of parameters for likelihood.

questions.question: What is a maximum-likelihood estimate \(\hat{\theta}\)?

options.text: The maximum numeric likelihood value
The parameter value that maximizes likelihood for the observed data
A posterior class probability
The number of observations

questions.explanation: An ML estimate is \(\hat{\theta}=\arg\max_\theta L(\theta:\mathcal{D})\), not the likelihood's maximum numeric value.

questions.question: A training set contains 60 bass and 40 salmon. What is the ML estimate of the prior \(P(\mathrm{bass})\)?
questions.explanation: For a discrete distribution, the ML estimate is the observed relative frequency.

questions.question: For a univariate Gaussian with unknown mean \(\mu\), what is the ML estimate \(\hat{\mu}\)?

options.text: The sample mean \(\frac{1}{N}\sum_i x_i\)
The sample maximum
Always zero
The number of samples

questions.explanation: The Gaussian mean that maximizes likelihood is the arithmetic mean of the observations.

questions.question: What does a single-Gaussian Bayes classifier assume for each class?

options.text: Each class-conditional density can be represented by one multivariate Gaussian
Every feature is a class label
All classes contain one training example
The decision boundary is always nonlinear

questions.explanation: The learner estimates one mean vector and covariance matrix for each class.

questions.question: Why can a single Gaussian be a poor class-conditional model?

options.text: It is always multimodal
Real class distributions may contain several distinct modes or subgroups
It cannot have a mean
It requires no parameters

questions.explanation: One Gaussian is unimodal and may not represent multiple separated clouds within a class.

questions.question: What assumption gives Naive Bayes its parameter-efficiency?

options.text: Features are conditionally independent given the class
All classes have probability zero
Every feature has the same observed value
The test set is used during training

questions.explanation: Conditional independence gives \(p(\mathbf{x}\mid\omega_k)=\prod_j p(x_j\mid\omega_k)\).

questions.question: If two features are strongly correlated within a class, what is a likely Naive Bayes problem?

options.text: It may produce inaccurate posterior probability estimates
It becomes a nearest-neighbour classifier
It cannot predict any class
It automatically learns the correlation matrix

questions.explanation: The independence model misrepresents correlated evidence, although classification can still work well.

questions.question: Why is Naive Bayes attractive for document classification with tens of thousands of word features?

options.text: It models the full exponential joint table
It estimates separate low-dimensional feature distributions efficiently
It requires dense documents
It ignores class priors

questions.explanation: Factorization avoids estimating a joint distribution over all word combinations.

questions.question: In fixed-radius nearest-neighbour density estimation, what happens if radius \(h\) is too small?

options.text: The estimate can be zero because the neighbourhood is empty
Every training point contributes equally
The estimate is always over-smoothed
Feature scaling becomes irrelevant

questions.explanation: A tiny neighbourhood may contain no observations, producing an unstable zero estimate.

questions.question: In fixed-radius nearest-neighbour density estimation, what happens if radius \(h\) is too large?

options.text: The estimate becomes overly blurred by distant points
The neighbourhood must be empty
The number of features becomes zero
The estimate becomes a posterior automatically

questions.explanation: Large neighbourhoods average over distant regions and erase local density structure.

questions.question: How does \(k\)-nearest-neighbour density estimation adapt to sparse regions?

options.text: It uses a larger radius to enclose the required \(k\) neighbours
It reduces the feature dimension to one
It duplicates the query point
It fixes the radius at zero

questions.explanation: The neighbourhood expands where data are sparse and contracts where data are dense.

questions.question: Why should features often be standardized before Euclidean-distance methods are applied?

options.text: Large-scale features would otherwise dominate the distance
Standardization creates class labels
Distances require probabilities summing to one
It guarantees no overfitting

questions.explanation: Centering and scaling put features on comparable units of standard deviation.

questions.question: What is the basic idea of kernel density estimation?

options.text: Each training example contributes a distance-decaying kernel to the density estimate
Only the nearest example contributes
A decision tree selects one feature
The density is assumed to be uniform

questions.explanation: The estimated density is an average of kernels centered on the observations.

questions.question: What is the effect of using a very wide Gaussian kernel?

options.text: A smoother but more blurred density estimate
A separate class for every point
A guaranteed zero estimate between points
A smaller training set

questions.explanation: Increasing bandwidth spreads each observation's contribution over a wider region.

questions.question: In a \(k\)-NN classifier, what estimates \(P(\omega_i\mid\mathbf{x})\)?

options.text: The fraction \(k_i/k\) of neighbours belonging to class \(\omega_i\)
The distance to the farthest point in the entire dataset
The global number of features
The likelihood maximum over \(\theta\)

questions.explanation: The local class frequency k_i/k directly estimates the class posterior around x.

questions.question: What is the explicit learning phase of the standard k-NN classifier?

options.text: Store the training set
Fit one covariance matrix
Optimize a separating hyperplane
Prune a tree

questions.explanation: k-NN is a lazy learner; most computation occurs when a query is classified.

questions.question: Which statement about k-NN prediction time is correct?

options.text: It generally grows with the size of the stored training set
It is independent of the amount of training data
It is always faster than a linear classifier
It requires no distance calculations

questions.explanation: A straightforward query compares the new point with stored examples.

questions.question: What is the curse of dimensionality for neighbour-based methods?

options.text: A fixed-size dataset becomes sparse and even nearest neighbours can be far away
More dimensions always make all points identical
The number of required examples decreases exponentially
Distances become exact class probabilities

questions.explanation: Maintaining local sample density requires exponentially more data as dimensionality grows.

questions.question: Why do irrelevant features particularly harm distance-based classifiers in high dimensions?

options.text: Their random distance contributions can obscure the relevant similarities
They are automatically assigned zero weight
They reduce the number of dimensions
They make all class priors uniform

questions.explanation: Distance treats included dimensions as evidence even when they carry no class information.
